## Two truths and a lie

An AI told me three things about R, very confidently.

1. R starts counting at 1, not 0.
2. `mean(c(1, 2, NA))` returns `1.5`.
3. `c(1, "a", TRUE)` turns everything into text.

. . .

::: {.vote}
Vote with fingers (1, 2, 3): which one is the lie?
:::

::: {.notes}
FLEX: skip if behind (saves about 4 min). Case #0 makes the same point.
:::

## The lie was #2

```{r}
c(10, 20, 30)[1]
mean(c(1, 2, NA))
c(1, "a", TRUE)
```

. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** A confident wrong answer looks exactly like a confident right one.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two truths and a lie: #2 is the lie (it returns NA). Don't explain NA yet, we come back to it in the essentials section.
:::

# Who's driving? {background-color="#f3f6ea"}

::: {.notes}
Target: start at 0:08, finish by 0:19. Framing plus the first live bug.
:::

## The new division of labor

**AI drives**: writes code fast

**You navigate**: choose the destination, read the map, check the route

. . .

Fast driving is great. Driving into a lake is not.

You can't catch a wrong turn on a map you can't read, so we learn to read R.

## What does a navigator do?

1. **Set the destination**: say clearly what you want
2. **Read the route**: understand the code
3. **Check the road**: run it, test it
4. **Make the call**: accept, fix, or reject

## The Audit Loop

1. **Read** it
2. **Run** it
3. **Restate** it in plain English
4. **Refine** it or **Reject** it

. . .

::: {.vote}
Restate is the superpower. If you can't say what a line does, you can't vouch for it.
:::

## Bug Bounty rules

- Every bug you catch: **+1 point** for your team
- Explain *why* an AI would make that mistake: **+1 bonus**
- Bugs hide in code **and** in answers that look fine

::: {.notes}
Keep the tally visible. Call on a different team each round.
:::

## Case #0: the request

> "Show me the 5 highest-rated movies on IMDb."

The AI wrote:

```{r}
#| eval: false
movies |>
  arrange(imdb_rating) |>
  select(title, imdb_rating) |>
  head(5)
```

::: {.vote}
With your partner (60 seconds): restate each line in plain English. Does it match the request? Navigator speaks, driver listens.
:::

## Run it: does this answer the request?

```{r}
#| echo: false
movies |>
  arrange(imdb_rating) |>
  select(title, imdb_rating) |>
  head(5)
```

::: {.vote}
Hands up: yes or no?
:::

. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** `arrange()` sorts ascending, so these are the five worst. No error, no warning, a clean table that looks right. Errors are the friendly failures.
:::

::: {.notes}
No. `arrange()` sorts ascending by default, so these are the five WORST rated (Disaster Movie 1.9, Epic Movie 2.3, Battlefield Earth 2.4, Viva Knievel! 2.7, Doogal 2.8). The code is on the previous slide: flip back if someone wants to see it. Fix later with `desc()`. Award points.
:::

# Reading the map {background-color="#f3f6ea"}

::: {.notes}

## Names and functions

```{r}
n_movies <- 651
n_movies
sqrt(16)
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
```

Read `<-` as "gets". A function has a name and arguments in parentheses.

## Vectors

A vector is a row of values of one type. `c()` combines.

```{r}
scores <- c(72, 88, 91, 65)
mean(scores)
scores * 2
```

## Three types you'll meet

```{r}
class(72)
class("Drama")
class(TRUE)
```

numeric, character, logical

## Yes/no questions

```{r}
scores > 70
sum(scores > 70)
```

`TRUE` counts as 1, so `sum()` counts the yeses.

## Challenge 1 (swap roles): predict first

```{r}
#| eval: false
genres <- c("Drama", "Comedy", "Horror")
genres == "Comedy"
genres %in% c("Drama", "Horror")
```

::: {.swap}
Navigator: predict both outputs out loud. Driver: type and run.
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
genres <- c("Drama", "Comedy", "Horror")
genres == "Comedy"
genres %in% c("Drama", "Horror")
```

`%in%` asks: "is each value anywhere in this set?"

::: {.notes}
Keep this one in mind: Case #1 (== vs %in%) depends on it.
:::

## NA means "I don't know"

Predict:

```{r}
#| eval: false
NA + 1
NA > 5
NA == NA
```

::: {.vote}
Vote: what do these print?
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
NA + 1
NA > 5
NA == NA
```

Is one unknown equal to another unknown? Unknown!

## Handling NA

```{r}
x <- c(4, 8, NA)
mean(x)
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
is.na(x)
```

. . .

::: {.bug}
`na.rm = TRUE` is a **decision**, not a fix. You chose to ignore the unknowns.
:::

::: {.notes}
Plant the seed: dropping missing values changes who is in your analysis. This returns in the WellSync cleaning sessions.
:::

## A column is a vector

```{r}
movies$runtime |> head(10)
```

`$` pulls one column out of a table.

## Mystery

```{r}
mean(movies$runtime)
```

. . .

::: {.vote}
Why NA? Talk to your partner (30 seconds).
:::

## Solving the mystery

```{r}
sum(is.na(movies$runtime))
mean(movies$runtime, na.rm = TRUE)
```

. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** One missing runtime made the whole mean unknown.
:::

::: {.notes}
If asked which movie it is: "The End of America". Finding it with brackets is in the Appendix and the handout; after `filter()` you can do it with `filter(is.na(runtime))`.
:::

# Verbs and the pipe {background-color="#f3f6ea"}

::: {.notes}
Target: start at 0:37, finish by 0:58. dplyr verbs and Bug Court. Cut material (Challenge 3, Case #2b) is in the Appendix and in the handout.
:::

## Data wrangling is a sentence

"Take movies, **then** keep the dramas, **then** sort by rating, **then** show the top 3."

. . .

The pipe `|>` reads as **then**.

## Same thing, two ways

```{r}
#| eval: false
head(arrange(filter(movies, genre == "Drama"), imdb_rating), 3)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
movies |>
  filter(genre == "Drama") |>
  arrange(imdb_rating) |>
  head(3)
```

You'll also see `%>%`, the older tidyverse pipe. It behaves the same for what we do.

::: {.notes}
In Positron the pipe shortcut is Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+M. A setting decides which pipe it inserts.
:::

## `select()`: choose columns

```{r}
movies |>
  select(title, genre, runtime, imdb_rating)
```

## `filter()`: keep rows

```{r}
movies |>
  select(title, genre, imdb_rating) |>
  filter(genre == "Drama")
```

## Conditions you can use

- `==` equal, `!=` not equal
- `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`
- `%in%` is in this set, `is.na()` is missing
- `,` or `&` means **and**; `|` means **or**

```{r}
movies |> filter(genre == "Drama", imdb_rating > 8) |> nrow()
```

::: {.notes}
Dramas rated above 8: 8 movies. Use it to show that a comma means "and".
:::

## Bug Court is in session

Each case: the request, the AI's code, and your verdict.

**Guilty** = it's wrong. **Innocent** = it's fine.

Use the Audit Loop. Restate before you vote.

## Case #1: the request

> "Keep the Drama and Comedy movies."

```{r}
#| eval: false
movies |>
  filter(genre == c("Drama", "Comedy"))
```

::: {.vote}
Restate it. Guilty or innocent?
:::

## Case #1: the evidence

```{r}
movies |> filter(genre == c("Drama", "Comedy")) |> nrow()
movies |> filter(genre %in% c("Drama", "Comedy")) |> nrow()
```

. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** `==` lines the two names up with rows one by one, back and forth. In your own console R also prints a warning. **Warnings are clues.**
:::

::: {.notes}
Guilty. 191 vs 392 rows. The recycling makes row 1 compare to "Drama", row 2 to "Comedy", row 3 to "Drama", and so on. Tie back to Challenge 1.
:::

## Case #2: the request

> "Keep movies that have a DVD release year."

```{r}
#| eval: false
movies |>
  filter(dvd_rel_year != NA)
```

::: {.vote}
Guilty or innocent?
:::

## Case #2: the evidence

```{r}
movies |> filter(dvd_rel_year != NA) |> nrow()
movies |> filter(!is.na(dvd_rel_year)) |> nrow()
```

. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** Anything compared with `NA` is `NA`, and `filter()` drops those. Zero rows, no error. The same thing happens quietly elsewhere: `filter(runtime > 0)` turns 651 rows into 650, because one runtime is `NA`.
:::

::: {.notes}
The 651 to 650 example (Case #2b) is in the Appendix with its code if you want to run it. This is the first appearance of "who disappears silently?", which becomes the cleaning impact audit in Lab 2.
:::

## Case #3: the request

> "How many documentaries are in the data?"

```{r}
#| eval: false
movies |>
  filter(genre == "Documentary") |>
  nrow()
```

::: {.vote}
Guilty or innocent? Look closely at the column names first.
:::

::: {.notes}
FLEX: skip Case #3 (both slides) if behind, saves about 3 min. The spec slide in Movie Night makes a similar point.
:::

## Case #3: the evidence

```{r}
movies |> filter(genre == "Documentary") |> nrow()
movies |> filter(title_type == "Documentary") |> nrow()
```

. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** The code is fine. The **question** was ambiguous. Two columns, two answers (52 vs 55).
:::

::: {.notes}
Neither answer is wrong. The navigator's job is to specify which column, or ask the AI which one it used. Great Week-3 theme: a good spec removes ambiguity.
:::

## `arrange()`: sort rows

Now fix Case #0.

```{r}
movies |>
  arrange(desc(imdb_rating)) |>
  select(title, imdb_rating)
```

## `mutate()`: make new columns

```{r}
movies |>
  mutate(runtime_hrs = runtime / 60) |>
  select(title, runtime, runtime_hrs)
```

## Four verbs, four jobs

- `select()` picks **columns**
- `filter()` keeps **rows**
- `arrange()` changes **order**
- `mutate()` makes **new columns**

# Movie Night {background-color="#f3f6ea"}

::: {.notes}
Target: start at 0:58, finish by 0:70. Teams of 3-4. Round 1 by hand (4 min), Round 2 with AI (6 min). Round 1 is the students' first hands-on filter practice, so circulate.

## How Movie Night works

Round 1: **by hand**.

Round 2: **with your AI**, and you audit it.

- Correct answer: **+1**
- Each bug you catch in the AI's code: **+1**

## Round 1 (by hand)

Among **R-rated Feature Films** longer than **150 minutes**, which has the **highest IMDb rating**?

::: {.swap}
Columns: `mpaa_rating`, `title_type`, `runtime`, `imdb_rating`. Hint: `filter()`, then `arrange(desc(...))`, then `head(1)`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Answer: The Godfather, Part II (202 min, IMDb 9.0). All six R-rated films over 150 minutes in this file are Feature Films, so the title_type condition doesn't change the result; still point out it is the safer spec.

Round 2 by hand (documentary with the lowest audience_score) is in the Appendix if you have extra time.
:::

## A good prompt is a spec

```
I have a tibble called `movies` with columns
title, studio, genre, runtime, imdb_rating.

Using dplyr and the |> pipe, find the studio with the
most movies.

Then explain each line in one plain-English sentence.
```

. . .

::: {.vote}
Data, task, tools, and ask for the explanation. The explanation feeds your Restate step.
:::

## Round 2 (with your AI)

Which **studio** released the most movies in this dataset?

1. Paste the spec into your AI
2. Run its code
3. **Audit Loop**: restate every line
4. Does the answer make sense? Hunt for bugs.

::: {.notes}
The AI will likely use `count()` or `group_by()` + `summarize()`: verbs students haven't met. That is the point: restate each step, ask the AI to explain, and check the answer by another route. Backup answer is in the appendix if no AI is available.

Correct answer: Paramount Pictures (37 movies). Bugs to listen for: ascending sort, an NA studio group sneaking in, or counting `distinct(studio)` instead of movies per studio.
:::

## Bug Bounty results

Which team has the most points?

. . .

Bugs from today:

- `arrange()` sorts **ascending** by default
- `NA` spreads through math
- `==` is not `%in%`
- `!= NA` never works
- Ambiguous questions get confident answers

**Audit Loop:** Read it, Run it, Restate it, Refine or Reject it.

## Moved: Case #2b, where did it go?

```{r}
nrow(movies)
movies |> filter(runtime > 0) |> nrow()
```

**Bug:** Every movie has a runtime above 0, yet one vanished: its runtime is `NA`. `filter()` **quietly drops** rows where the condition is `NA`.

## Backup: AI answer for Round 2

Use this if no AI is available. Audit it!

```{r}
#| eval: false
movies |>
  group_by(studio) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  arrange(n) |>
  head(1)
```

::: {.notes}
Same bug as Case #0 in a new costume: `arrange(n)` is ascending, so this returns a studio with a single movie. Fix: `arrange(desc(n))`. Pattern: AI repeats failure modes, so learn the common ones.
:::

## Backup: running it

```{r}
movies |>
  group_by(studio) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  arrange(n) |>
  head(1)
```

## Backup: the fix

```{r}
movies |>
  group_by(studio) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(1)
```
